source.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Channels in Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Robin Hesse; Jonas Fischer; Simone Schaub-Meyer; Stefan Roth

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a method can separate polysemantic channels using a weight-restructuring approach and activation measurements, rather than measuring neuron-explanation quality as in the claim's original audit.
record.gate_note: The reported quantitative outcomes are the relative activations of disentangled and residual channels. Hyperparameter choices and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows. The study does not estimate the overall share of interpretable channels.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a weight-restructuring tool that splits γ-polysemantic channels in one ResNet-50 layer and reports only that tool's activation separation (Table 1). It reports no share of interpretable channels, no count of polysemantic channels, and no comparison across architectures or tools. It is a mitigation method evaluated on its own performance, so it does not test V4 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors present a proof-of-concept tool that identifies and disentangles γ-polysemantic channels into single-concept channels. They say it does not apply directly to other forms of polysemanticity, uses handpicked hyperparameters, and may work better in later layers. They do not estimate how common polysemantic or interpretable channels are.
record.recipe_differences: The study restructures CNN weights to split channels and assesses activation separation; it does not use the original language-model neuron-audit method or score explanations on new text.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that results depend on handpicked, application-specific τ, γ, and p thresholds; their experiments focus on the last convolutional layer and two-concept cases.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet-50's last convolutional layer, channels flagged as γ-polysemantic (γ=0.5) can be split by weight editing into two channels, each mainly active for one class concept (114% vs −9%; −21% vs 125%), with a residual channel near 0% (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some polysemantic CNN channels can be explicitly disentangled into monosemantic channels by editing weights, without changing network output.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper separates channels relevant to two classes into a shared-concept case (e.g., dog species, high ARV similarity) and a polysemantic case (low ARV similarity, low WordNet similarity) (Fig. 4). It gives no counts or rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many multi-class channels reflect a shared concept rather than polysemanticity; this is related to V3 but no share is reported.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
record.problems: The evidence is limited to one pretrained architecture and its last convolutional layer, with handpicked hyperparameters and no reported uncertainty. The quantitative table aggregates across identified polysemantic channels without stating their number. Predictive-performance preservation is asserted as a property of the method but is not reported as a measured result here.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level shares (one job, two related jobs, not understood).
Shares across language models, dense or MoE, and across scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose as a shared feature, recursive generalization versus superposition.
The share of interpretable neurons and whether it rises with better tools or modern architectures; architecture or regularization as causes; the essay's InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out data.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V4 'supports' label are not justified. V4 concerns the share of interpretable neurons rising with tools or architecture, and this paper reports neither a share nor a comparison, only its own tool's separation quality on an unstated number of channels. Preservation of predictive performance is asserted by construction but not measured.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level proportions and the shares with one job, two related jobs, or no understood job.
Comparable shares across language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, whether it represents pose, and recursive generalization versus superposition.

The study tests whether its tool can disentangle channels in one ResNet-50 setting. It does not test architecture or regularization as causes, compare architectures or tools, or estimate an overall interpretable-neuron share or the stated InceptionV1-sized-model estimates.
Attribution graphs, circuit explanations of model behaviour, and comparisons with trained replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether an explanation written from activating examples predicts firing on examples it was not written from.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: ImageNet-trained ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Restructured weights to split each identified polysemantic channel into two concept channels and a residual channel; measured relative activation on evaluation images.

conditions.value: reported aggregate over polysemantic channels; number of channels not stated

rows.measure: Mean relative activation versus the original channel
rows.note: The paper reports this as the aggregate activation for the first disentangled channel on first-class images.
rows.check: This is the study's own method performance (disentangled channel 1 on concept-1 images, 114%). It is not a measure of the share of interpretable neurons, nor of whether that share rises with tools or architecture.
